dimming.blocksAllPattern: {{planet}} is as big as the star and hides all of it.
dimming.dragHint: Drag the planet across the star.
dimming.explanationTitle: Why does the star get dimmer?
dimming.explanation1: When a planet passes between its star and us, it covers a small part of the star. That part's light never reaches us, so the star looks a little dimmer. Astronomers call this a transit.
dimming.explanation2: The bigger the planet compared with its star, the more light it blocks. Jupiter would block about 1 % of the Sun's light; Earth only about 0.008 %, less than 1 part in 10 000.
dimming.explanation3: A small star makes the same planet easier to find: Earth in front of a red dwarf five times smaller than the Sun blocks 25 times more of the star's light.
dimming.explanation4: Real stars are so far away that telescopes see them as points. We never see the planet itself: we find it because its star dims, again and again, every time the planet goes around.
dimming.keyboardHelpMove: Move the planet along its orbit

screenSummary.playArea: The play area shows a planet orbiting its star twice: seen from the side, and seen from Earth, zoomed in. A chart traces how bright the star looks over time.
screenSummary.controlArea: The control area has radio buttons to choose the planet and the star, a slider for a planet of any size, a telescope-view checkbox, time controls, an explanation button, and a Reset All button.
screenSummary.interactionHint: Play the animation, or move the planet with the arrow keys, and watch the brightness drop while the planet is in front of the star. Try a smaller planet or a smaller star.

dimming.currentDetailsPattern: {{planet}} orbits a star with {{starRadius}} times the Sun's radius. At most it blocks {{percent}} percent of the star's light. The star's brightness is now {{brightness}} percent; the planet is {{where}}.
